chapter: The craft of the ad lib player
title: The uncertainties an ad lib player faces on every job
summary: Hall speaks about not knowing the drummer or the pay when going to an engagement.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Now, to get back to -- to that other direction we're talking in about atmosphere, you know,

that the musician plays in, which just doesn't mean, you know, the physical layout of a club, but the whole business of music into which the ad lib player, as you refer to them, is thrown. You know, comment on this, as you want to.

Well, you rev yourself up to go on an engagement. You don't know what you're going to run into, as far as getting there, for one, and being received is another, and getting paid is another. And all these things can be negative, but you start out the door more or less trying to think of how you're going to perform.

Being an ad lib person, you go with different groups, so you can't possibly foretell what that's going to be when you leave home. Maybe you'll have a compatible drummer. Maybe you'll have a jerk. That's -- so that's going to destroy your night right off.
But even when you're working with a set group as you have on many occasions for months on end, there are the other factors, those extra-musical factors which come into consideration.
